title: Al-Asma'i and the Three Scholars of Basra

keywords: al-asma'i and the three girls of bassorah
full_text:
Al-Asma'i, the celebrated philologist and literary master of Baghdad, was visiting the garden city of Basra to collect rare words and dialect proverbs. While walking through a quiet orchard of pomegranate and fig trees, he heard three youthful voices debating the subtle grammatical meters of classical poetry from behind a flowering jasmine hedge.

The voices belonged to three intelligent young maidens who were daughters of the city’s chief grammarian. They were composing verses describing the setting sun and the evening star.

Al-Asma'i, unable to resist testing their learning, stepped into the arbor and recited a challenging classical hemistich with an archaic, obscure grammatical construction:
'The shadows lengthen as the day grows pale...'

The first maiden immediately answered without a second's hesitation, completing the meter with flawless rhyme:
'And stars unfold their silver on the veil!'

The second maiden added with sparkling wit:
'While scholars wander through the dusty road,'

And the third maiden completed the stanza with a teasing bow:
'To gather verses for their royal code!'

Al-Asma'i laughed aloud with boundless delight, astonished that three young girls in an orchard could match the most intricate meters of classical poetry with such effortless perfection and playful charm.

The master grammarian bowed low before the three scholars and declared: 'For forty years I have traveled from oasis to oasis collecting the treasures of the Arabic tongue; but today in Basra, I have found that the purest fountain of language flows from the lips of our youth!' He recorded their verses in his grand anthology, which was preserved for centuries in the libraries of Baghdad.
moral: Linguistic brilliance and cultivated wit among youth are the truest ornaments of a civilized society.
